subtype: Approach: breaking cleaning his room into small jobs [Thinking]
passage: I'm Gautam. Last Sunday my room looked as if a storm had passed. Socks on the fan, comics under the chair, cars in a heap. I stood at the door and wanted to go back to bed. Then I said to myself: one thing at a time. First just clothes, all the clothes, into the cupboard or the basket. Done. Then books, on the shelf. Then toys, in the box. Last, the floor, with the broom. Each time I finished a part, the mess got smaller. After forty minutes, Nitin looked in and said, "Who cleaned this?" I said, "Me, one bit at a time."

qa.q: What did Gautam do first when cleaning?
qa.a: Gautam put the clothes in the cupboard or the basket first.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel at the door of the messy room?
qa.a: Gautam felt overwhelmed and wanted to go back to bed, until splitting the job into parts made it seem smaller.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gautam use, and why?
qa.a: Gautam could put everything on the bed and sort it into piles, or race a timer. Both make the job clearer or more fun, so it feels less heavy.

qa.q: How might Nitin see the tidy room?
qa.a: Nitin looked in and asked who had cleaned, so Nitin was surprised and probably impressed that the storm-hit room was neat.

grounding: A boy overwhelmed by a messy room splits it into clothes, books, toys and floor and does one at a time, so the mess shrinks with each finished part.
